20583-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India is a large official survey of the peoples of central India. Compiled under British rule, it describes tribe by tribe, caste by caste, their customs, gods, work, and kinship rules. Each group gets its own careful entry.

A note singles out the Gonds as the most important of the non-Aryan or primitive tribes, whose social customs are described in detail. The Baiga, Bhil, Kawar, Khond, Kol, Korku, and Korwa stand among the other major tribes covered. Whatever its colonial frame, the survey preserves a vast record of Indian social life.
20668-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
This volume of The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India continues the great ethnographic survey of the region. Entries describe each tribe and caste: its legends, marriages, funerals, gods, and work. The volume opens with help for readers facing Indian words in English letters.

Its pronunciation key explains that one a has the sound of u in but or murmur. Another a sounds as in bath or tar. The letter e matches the sound in the French word écarté, and i may sound as in bit. With that key, readers could speak the names of the Gonds, Bhils, and hundreds of smaller groups the survey records.
22010-the-tribes-and-castes-of-the-centr:
R. V. Russell of the Indian Civil Service directed the ethnographic survey of India's Central Provinces. Working with Rai Bahadur Hira Lal, he produced The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India in four volumes, printed in 1916. Volume II runs through the alphabet from the Agaria iron-workers onward. Each article treats one caste or tribe in turn.

Entries describe a group's work, customs, marriage rules, gods, and place in village life. Herdsmen, merchants, forest tribes, robbers turned labourers, and holy beggars all appear. The book was an official record, made so district officers could know the people they governed. Today it stands as a vast, flawed snapshot of Indian society under British rule.
22172-the-knickerbocker-or-new-york-mont:
The Knickerbocker was New York's leading literary monthly in the 1840s. This number, volume 23 for May 1844, opens with Thomas Carlyle on Napoleon Bonaparte. The editors compiled the piece from Carlyle's works, offering all he had published on Napoleon in one place. It stands in for a fuller article they could not get.

Around it sit poems, tales, reviews, and the editor's table talk that made the magazine famous. The Knickerbocker published Irving's circle and set New York's literary tone for a generation. A single issue preserves that tone: ambitious, clubbable, and proud of American letters. It also shows how American magazines fed readers on British lions like Carlyle.
22402-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science mixed essays, fiction, and bold ideas. One passage dreams of a cloud observed hanging over Washington. The writer would annex it by electrical communications in every direction.

A resident governor would sit fixed at the cloud's center in a balloon. The same pages turn to France and Algeria with equal confidence. France has gorged Kabylia, the writer says, but never digested it. Such leaps show the magazine's free-ranging nineteenth-century mind. Science, empire, and fancy shared its pages without apology. Readers get a period monthly in full flight, part journal and part speculation.
23095-lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-l:
Kabylia opens this volume of Lippincott's Magazine of Popular Literature and Science. The inhabitants of Kalaa pass for rich, a traveler writes. Kalaa's women walk unveiled and jeweled, its streets unusually clean for Kabylia. Four sheikhs govern the place, and the travelers carry an introduction to one of them.

Their safe-conduct, the anaya, holds good. An imposing elder in a white burnoose receives the party with warmth under a stately manner. Travel, fiction, poetry, and science share Lippincott's pages in the Philadelphia monthly's usual blend. A bound volume like this one was a middle-class library in itself. Its Algerian journey shows the reach of its curiosity, and its confidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cefalu: A 1913 entry on Cefalù — the Sicilian diocese. Umberto Benigni gives its Norman story. Its cathedral's Christ crowns the apse. The rock guards the fishing town. A see of the island's north. Its Norman cloister is famed.
doe-osti-2997579-de-novo-synthesis-and-n: Immune receptors got synthesized and imaged, and this DOE report covers de novo host proteins. The pages detail the near-atomic imaging. The biologists get their structures. The receptors were immune. The imaging was near-atomic. The biologists got structures.

The molecules were value added. The closeout was chemist. The added were value. The final were CRADA. The molecules were development.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KORLHonolulu_KO:
Harold Weisberg wrote on December 6, 1974 to Buck Buchanan of KORL Radio in Honolulu. He thanked Buchanan for the airtime the station had given him. Weisberg also describes the six thousand dollars he had borrowed to print his book, the debt behind the publicity tour.

Radio was how a self-published researcher reached the country, station by station. A thank-you letter to a Honolulu host maps that circuit at its farthest reach. The borrowed printing money in the same letter shows what the circuit cost the man who traveled it.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The June 1875 Lippincott's, Volume Fifteen, Number 90, travels widely. A concluding paper goes up the Paraná and into Paraguay. E. C. Grenville Murray tells a tale of the conscription. Sidney Lanier contributes a poem called The Symphony.

William Black's Three Feathers advances through chapters thirty-six to forty. Laura Winthrop Johnson begins Eight Hundred Miles in an Ambulance. Lawrence Turnbull reviews Mill's essays on religion. Monthly gossip ranges from women's rights to Japanese art. Camp-fire lyrics and a scene in the Campagna add verse and travel. Our monthly gossip visits Lorenzo de' Medici's tomb too.
mabel-martin-a-harvest-idyl-and-other-po:
Mabel Martin is a narrative poem by John Greenleaf Whittier, the Quaker poet. This part comes from the first volume of his collected works. Whittier's note recalls Susanna Martin, hanged for witchcraft at Amesbury. Her daughter is the witch's daughter of his harvest idyl.

The poem moves from the river valley to a husking bee. A champion stands up for the shunned and slandered girl. Shadow lifts, and a betrothal closes the story in light. Other poems here include 'The Prophecy of Samuel Sewall' and 'Cobbler Keezar's Vision.' Whittier loved New England legend and plain country folk. His ballads keep colonial history alive in song.
nasa-tm-19670010329-the-fabrication-of-b:
R. F. Williams and S. E. Ingels, of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, wrote this volume in July 1966. Numbered TM X-53453, it is Volume II of a six-volume set on fabricating beryllium. Beryllium is a very light but difficult metal, prized for aerospace vehicle structures. This volume covers forming techniques for beryllium alloys.

The report documents forming methods studied and developed for building beryllium structures. Time and temperature links are set down for straight bends, compound curved channels, and half-round segments. The flow of the material during forming is traced, and the size changes that result are measured. Extreme forming of cross-rolled beryllium sheet is also shown to work. Companion volumes survey current technology and cover metal removal, surface treatments, thermal treatments, and joining.
nasa-tm-19710018652-feasibility-study-of:
Francis S Stepka and Rene E Chambellan of the Lewis Research Center issued this feasibility study in June 1971. It designs a plug nozzle for an afterburning turbojet that is cooled by its own jet fuel. Fuel flowing through the nozzle walls would carry heat away before burning. The team weighed cooling power, fuel coking, construction, and strength.

Their design study found the engine's full fuel flow could do the job. Metal touching the fuel would stay at or below a set temperature limit. At that heat, coke deposits inside the cooling tubes looked unlikely to matter. Test results from other workers supported at least one hundred hours of running. The nozzle concept passed its feasibility check.
nasa-tm-19720008686-radiofrequency-sputt:
Talivaldis Spalvins of the Lewis Research Center described this coating method in February 1972, as NASA TM X-2498. Radiofrequency sputtering knocks atoms off a target so they settle as a thin film. Odd shaped parts are hard to coat evenly by most methods. Bearings, seals, and gears all have hidden faces that still need lubricant films. Spalvins showed that sputtering can reach every face at once.

Placed correctly near the target, a part coats on all sides. Shape does not block the coverage. The film formed is dense and sticks well. Its thickness varied by a fifth to a half across a bearing cage. Working films of dry lubricant need be only thousands of atoms thick. Only the contact spots truly need that coverage.
podcast-dannyjones-dloU2GQ7FlU:
Cult expert Rick Ross joins Danny Jones to explain how to free people from brainwashing by cults. Ross has spent decades doing this work and has faced cult members in tense rooms. Jones hosts the talk and draws out his methods.

Ross walks through how deprogramming works, from the first family call to the long talks that break a group's hold. He shares hard cases and the risks that come with the work. Jones asks what signs mark a group as a cult. Listeners get a rare guide to a strange trade, told by a man known for it across the country.
podcast-joerogan-_kDKAOncclU:
Geographer Bradley Garrett joins the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 1515 to talk about urban exploring. Garrett wrote a book on place hacking, the art of entering the hidden city: rooftops, drains, and ruins behind fences. His research took him into tunnels under London and beyond.

He tells Rogan what draws explorers down and up into forbidden space, and what those places teach about the cities above them. Rogan asks about the arrests, the falls, and the ethics of trespass as research. The episode is a thrilling tour of the secret city, led by a man who mapped it with his own feet.
podcast-joerogan-tznvMq2v5lU:
Writer Alex Berenson returns to the Joe Rogan Experience for episode 2037 to press his pandemic dissent. Berenson, a former New York Times reporter and novelist, became famous for questioning lockdowns and vaccine claims. His views got him banned from Twitter before he was restored.

Berenson goes through the data he says officials and media got wrong. He talks about his books and posts on cannabis and COVID that made him a hero to skeptics and a villain to others. Rogan asks about censorship and the cost of speaking out. The episode is Berenson unfiltered, at full length.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JZxj_c0g5lU:
Tucker Carlson responds to Israel's war on Iran in this episode of direct commentary. Carlson broke with many on his own side by opposing American support for the strikes. His take is presented as a lonely dissent while the bombs fall.

Carlson lays out why he believes the war does not serve American interests. He questions the claims made for the strikes and the push to draw in US forces. The episode argues for restraint in the plainest terms he can muster. Concerned and peace-minded viewers get the host's case against a war his movement largely cheered.
the-emigrants-of-ahadarra-the-works-of-w:
William Carleton's The Emigrants of Ahadarra opens on a summer morning at a strong farmer's house in Ireland. A small man in beggar's dress walks up with a slim girl of about sixteen, toward a house set on a rise some hundreds of yards from the highway. Carleton notes its look of plenty mixed with slovenly neglect, which he calls a sad mark of his country.

A rusty iron gate, too hard to open or shut, has worn side paths through the hedge. Rich farmer, beggar, and girl meet at that gate. Carleton sets a tale of pride, debt, and flight to America.
the-variation-of-animals-and-plants-unde: Darwin’s second volume piles proof from farm and garden. Pigeons, dogs, and wheat all argue for selection. The Origin’s vast storehouse of fact, the Origin's vast storehouse of fact, proof from farm and garden.
